title: Swedish researchers build AI that runs biology lab with oversight
source_used: The Brighter Side of News (also read Bioengineer.org)
key_facts: Chalmers University of Technology (Sweden) built a closed-loop AI system that generates biology hypotheses, plans experiments, directs lab robots, analyses results and refines later questions.
Tested on brewer's yeast, Saccharomyces cerevisiae; published in the Journal of the Royal Society Interface.
Hybrid design: about 60,000 structured relationships about yeast, inductive logic programming (735 logic programs generated) and a language model that designs interventions.
Produced 1,933 candidate hypotheses involving 16 amino acids; five amino acids (glutamate, arginine, proline, glutamine, lysine) were tested under chemical stress.
Some hypotheses held (arginine plus caffeine slowed growth more than expected), others failed (arginine did not rescue cells from lithium stress); failures were stored.
Per Brighter Side, aminoadipate partly protected cells from formic acid stress; humans still handled some physical tasks and set research limits.
quote_evidence: Researchers at Chalmers University of Technology developed a closed-loop system that can generate biological hypotheses, decide how to test them, translate those plans into machine-readable instructions, analyze experimental results and use the findings to refine later questions.
The laboratory was not completely autonomous, because humans still handled some physical tasks and set research boundaries.
why_it_matters_hint: A lab loop that links reasoning to real experiments, with humans still setting limits.
event_date: Study published in the Journal of the Royal Society Interface; coverage dated 2 Oct 2026
